old:
- 16x Stat cubes (white) (Core)
- 8x Hollow cubes
- 1x Spark dial (Core)
new:
- 16x Stat cubes (white) (Core)
- 1x Spark dial (Core)
rationale: Hollow cubes are not a separate component; they are the white cubes of the core set that are not marking a stat, so the unsourced line is removed.
evidence: Core 2017 component list: 16x Level Up Tokens (white cubes), DS-Core-Rules-lores.txt l.244; author's source 03_characters.md l.58 and 07_gameplay.md l.20 ('white cubes').

old: *Hollow cubes* are of a colour distinct from the damage, stamina, and stat cubes; two are placed on the endurance bar of a character who is *hollow* (see §7.2).
new: *Hollow cubes* are white cubes that are not in use as stat cubes; two are placed on the endurance bar of a character who is *hollow* (see §7.2). A white cube is placed on an endurance bar for no other purpose, so a hollow cube cannot be taken for a damage cube or a stamina cube. The supply of white cubes is not a limit: when every white cube is in use, the players mark the blocked spaces with any other markers that are neither red nor black.
rationale: Names the physical component (white cube, never otherwise on the endurance bar) and gives the fallback for a party of four, whose 16 white cubes are all stat cubes.
evidence: Author's source ('a marker such as white cubes'); Extended Rules l.57-59 (a marker of any type when the box lacks a colour); §2.8 already treats the soul token supply the same way.

old: **Hollow cube.** One of eight cubes of a colour distinct from the damage, stamina, and stat cubes. Two *hollow cubes* block the two rightmost spaces of a hollow character's endurance bar.
new: **Hollow cube.** A white cube placed on an endurance bar. Two *hollow cubes* block the two rightmost spaces of a hollow character's endurance bar. Hollow cubes are taken from the white cubes that are not in use as *stat cubes* (see §2.8).
rationale: Definition follows the component ruling.

old: **Hollow cube.** One of eight cubes of a colour distinct from the damage, stamina, and stat cubes. Two hollow cubes block the two rightmost spaces of a *hollow* character's endurance bar (see §7.2).
new: **Hollow cube.** A white cube, taken from the white cubes that are not in use as stat cubes, placed on an endurance bar. Two hollow cubes block the two rightmost spaces of a *hollow* character's endurance bar (see §2.8, §7.2).
rationale: Glossary follows the component ruling.

old: 3. Arrange the bonfire tile, the four encounter tiles, and the mini-boss tile, which is one of the two *boss tiles* (see §15.3), in a grid of two rows of three tiles, with the bonfire tile and the mini-boss tile in opposite corners.
new: 3. Lay the bonfire tile, the four encounter tiles, and the mini-boss tile, which is one of the two *boss tiles* (see §15.3), in a single chain, each tile beside the next, with the bonfire tile at one end and the mini-boss tile at the other. The chain may run straight or turn at any tile, as the table allows; two rows of three tiles, with the bonfire tile and the mini-boss tile in opposite corners, form one such chain.
rationale: One layout rule for both legs: the route is a chain of tiles and its shape is free; the two-by-three grid stays as a permitted arrangement.
evidence: Official 2017 setup lays the tiles 'in any way you wish, aligning their doorways as you go' (DS-Core-Rules-lores.txt l.295-300); findings A-088, C-090, D-031 disagree only about shape.

old: 4. Turn each encounter tile so that exactly two of its doorways open on to adjacent tiles, forming a single route from the bonfire tile through all four encounter tiles to the mini-boss tile.
new: 4. Turn each encounter tile so that one of its doorways faces the tile before it in the chain and another faces the tile after it, forming a single route from the bonfire tile through all four encounter tiles to the mini-boss tile. A doorway that faces neither of those tiles is not used.
rationale: 'Exactly two doorways' cannot be met by a tile with three or four doorways placed in a grid; the route is fixed by the chain, and spare doorways are ignored.
evidence: Official tiles carry differing numbers of doorways (DS-Core-Rules-lores.txt l.409, l.835-850).

old: 6. Arrange the *bonfire* tile, the four encounter tiles, and the main-boss tile in a straight line, with the bonfire tile and the main-boss tile at opposite ends. The main-boss tile is the two *boss tiles* joined as one (see §15.3).
new: 6. Lay the *bonfire* tile, the four encounter tiles, and the main-boss tile in a single chain, as in the first setup (see §6.5, Encounter Tiles), with the bonfire tile at one end and the main-boss tile at the other. The main-boss tile is the two *boss tiles* joined as one (see §15.3).
rationale: Second leg uses the same chain rule as the first; a straight line of seven tile widths is no longer required.

old:
13. Deal one *tier two treasure* card per character face down to each encounter tile. These cards are the encounter's treasure reward (see §7.7).
14. If mimics are in play, deal one ambush card face down beside each encounter tile (see §13).
15. If *invaders* are in play, place the *invader tokens* on the encounter cards (see §12.2).
16. Restock the tier one *shop* and stock the tier two shop (see §6.3, Restocking After a Boss).
new:
13. Restock the tier one *shop* and stock the tier two shop (see §6.3, Restocking After a Boss).
14. Deal one *tier two treasure* card per character face down to each encounter tile. These cards are the encounter's treasure reward (see §7.7).
15. If mimics are in play, deal one ambush card face down beside each encounter tile (see §13).
16. If *invaders* are in play, place the *invader tokens* on the encounter cards (see §12.2).
rationale: The shop is stocked before the treasure rewards are dealt, as in the first setup (§6.3 before §6.5), so the five legendary cards are in the tier two deck when the second leg's rewards are dealt.
evidence: Official 2017 adds the legendary cards to the deck when the mini-boss falls so that they can be drawn in the second half (DS-Core-Rules-lores.txt l.371-381); author's source: legendary treasure 'do not appear in every game'.

old:
7. If the *shop* has not been restocked since a boss was last defeated, restock it (see §6.3, Restocking After a Boss).
8. The characters may visit the *Firekeeper* (see §11.3) and Blacksmith Andre (see §11.4), in either order and any number of times.
9. *Reset* every encounter (see §11.5).
new:
7. The characters may visit the *Firekeeper* (see §11.3) and Blacksmith Andre (see §11.4), in either order and any number of times.
8. *Reset* every encounter (see §11.5).
rationale: The conditional restock never takes effect: the setup after a boss (§6.6, §6.7) and the setup of a campaign section (§18.6) restock before the rest begins.
evidence: §6.6 step 16, §6.7 step 7, §18.6; chapter 11 issues list, item 7.

old: Resting does not restock the shop except as step 7 directs. Cards bought from the shop are not replaced, and unsold cards stay in the shop, until the shop is next restocked (see §6.3, Restocking After a Boss). In campaign play, step 7 applies when a section has been completed rather than when a boss has been defeated (see §18.6, Blacksmith Andre's Shop).
new: Resting does not restock the *shop*. Cards bought from the shop are not replaced, and unsold cards stay in the shop, until the shop is next restocked during the setup that follows a boss's defeat (see §6.3, Restocking After a Boss). In campaign play the shop is restocked during the setup that follows the completion of a section (see §18.6, Blacksmith Andre's Shop).
rationale: Follows the deletion of step 7.

old: Before the shop is restocked, its unsold cards, other than *ember cards*, are placed on the bottom of their treasure decks (see §6.3, Restocking After a Boss). Step 7 of a rest restocks the shop only if a section has been completed and the shop has not been restocked since (see §11.2).
new: Before the shop is restocked, its unsold cards, other than *ember cards*, are placed on the bottom of their treasure decks (see §6.3, Restocking After a Boss).
rationale: Removes the reference to the deleted step.

old: They are flipped back to the ready side only when the characters rest at the *bonfire* (see §11.2). Clearing an encounter does not ready them (see §7.5, Encounter Recovery).
new: They are flipped back to the ready side only when the characters rest at the *bonfire* (see §11.2), so each is used at most once between rests. Clearing an encounter does not ready them (see §7.5, Encounter Recovery).
rationale: The one refresh rule of the three tokens is stated once, with its consequence, in the paragraph that covers all three.
evidence: Official 2017 and 2022 ready all three tokens at the bonfire rest (DS-Core-Rules-lores.txt l.702-706; DS-TG-Rulebook l.1929-1933).

old: The printed wording of a heroic action overrides any other rule with which it conflicts. The token is readied only at the bonfire, so a character resolves the heroic action at most once between rests.
new: The printed wording of a heroic action overrides any other rule with which it conflicts.
rationale: Removes a restatement of the shared refresh rule so that the three token sub-sections are parallel.

old:
Condition tokens are not removed.

The estus flask token is not readied when an encounter is *cleared*. It is flipped to the ready side only when the characters rest at the bonfire (see §11.2).
new: Condition tokens are not removed.
rationale: Removes a restatement of the shared refresh rule so that the three token sub-sections are parallel.

old: 3. Give each character, including each character who died, one of the treasure cards dealt to the tile (see §7.7).
new: 3. Award the treasure cards dealt to the tile, one to each character, including each character who died; where a single card was dealt to the tile, award it to the party (see §7.7).
rationale: Step 3 now also fits the Level 4 encounter, to which one card is dealt for the whole party (§6.7).

old: The players decide which character takes which card; if they cannot agree, the character holding the *aggro token* decides.
new: The cards are turned face up, and the players decide which character takes which card; if they cannot agree, the character holding the *aggro token* decides.
rationale: States that the dealt cards are revealed before they are shared out.

old: A treasure card a character receives is placed in that character's inventory (see §4.1).
new: A treasure card a character receives is placed in that character's inventory (see §3.2).
rationale: The inventory is defined in §3.2, not §4.1.

old: After rolling the dice for one of their own attack rolls or defence rolls (a *block*, *resist*, or *dodge* roll), a character may flip the luck token to the used side to reroll any or all of those dice.
new: After rolling the dice for one of their own attack rolls or defence rolls (a *block*, *resist*, *dodge*, or *parry* roll), a character may flip the luck token to the used side to reroll any or all of those dice.
rationale: §9.6 already allows the luck token on a parry roll; the list in §3.5 omitted it.

old: 4. Place the character's *luck*, *heroic action*, and *estus flask* tokens on the dashboard, ready side up (see §3.5).
new: 4. Place the character's *luck*, *heroic action*, and *estus flask* tokens on the dashboard, ready side up, and the character's *ember* token beside the dashboard (see §3.5).
rationale: §3.5 and the glossary start the ember token beside the dashboard; §6.1 placed it in the common supply.
evidence: CMP-0001 (approved at Gate 1): 'The ember token begins the game beside the dashboard'.

old: 5. Place the *ember* tokens, *damage cubes*, *stamina cubes*, *hollow cubes*, soul tokens, *condition* tokens, *trap tokens*, and *wound tokens* in a supply within reach of every player (see §2.8).
new: 5. Place the *damage cubes*, *stamina cubes*, remaining white cubes, soul tokens, *condition* tokens, *trap tokens*, and *wound tokens* in a supply within reach of every player (see §2.8). The remaining white cubes serve as *hollow cubes* (see §7.2).
rationale: Ember tokens leave the common supply (core-019) and the hollow cubes are named as the spare white cubes (core-001).

old: 2. Discard the character's *ember token*, if present (see §7.3).
new: 2. Remove the character's *ember token* from the dashboard, if present, and place it beside the dashboard (see §7.3).
rationale: Matches §3.5: the token is the character's own and returns to its place beside the dashboard.

old: their souls are dropped, their ember token is discarded, and their model is placed beside the bonfire tile
new: their souls are dropped, their ember token is removed, and their model is placed beside the bonfire tile
rationale: Same wording as the death procedure.

old: 1. Discard the ember card.
new: 1. Return the ember card to the game box. It takes no further part in the game.
rationale: States where a consumed ember card goes; the supply of one per character at setup is the limit on embering by card.
evidence: §6.3 (one ember card per character, never restocked; A-046); chapter 04 and chapter 07 issues lists.

old: A character consumes an ember card by discarding it from the back-up slot, as the *Ember* major action during an encounter or at any time outside an encounter.
new: A character consumes an ember card by discarding it from the back-up slot, as the *Ember* major action during an encounter or at any time outside an encounter. The consumed card is returned to the game box and takes no further part in the game.
rationale: Same destination stated where the ember card is described.

old: **Ember card.** A tier one shop card. Discarding an *ember* card from the back-up slot (the *Ember* major action, or outside an encounter) makes the character *embered* (see §7.3). A character may carry only one *ember* card and cannot carry one while *embered*; a card held when the character becomes *embered* passes to another character (see §7.3).
new: **Ember card.** A tier one shop card. Discarding an *ember* card from the back-up slot (the *Ember* major action, or outside an encounter) makes the character *embered*, and the card is returned to the game box (see §7.3). A character may carry only one *ember* card and cannot carry one while *embered*; a card held when the character becomes *embered* passes to another character (see §7.3).
rationale: Glossary follows §7.3.

old: Spells are never *two-handed*: a spell gains no two-handed reroll, and a spell equipped with the other weapon slot empty is not two-handed (see §10.4).
new: Spells are never *two-handed*: a spell gains no two-handed reroll, and a spell equipped with the other weapon slot empty is not two-handed (see §10.4). A spell card that bears the two-handed weapon icon requires the other weapon slot to be empty while it is equipped in a weapon slot (see §3.2), and it gains no reroll by this.
rationale: Separates the slot a spell occupies (its printed icon) from the two-handed reroll (never for spells).
evidence: §3.2 weapon slots; chapter 04 issues list, item 7.

old: A card's stat requirements also decide its treasure tier, split at a requirement of 25 (see §6.2).
new: A card's stat requirements also decide its treasure tier, split at a requirement of 25 (see §6.2). The stat requirements of the weapons listed in Appendix A are those given there, in place of the printed values (see Appendix A).
rationale: The main text never told the reader that Appendix A replaces printed requirements.

old: Treasure cards from every expansion in the party's collection are included and are sorted into the tier one and tier two treasure decks by the rules of this section.
new: Treasure cards from every expansion in the party's collection are included and are sorted into the tier one and tier two treasure decks by the rules of this section. The cards listed in Appendix B are added or amended as that appendix states before the decks are built (see Appendix B).
rationale: Setup now points to the card amendments it depends on.

old: 2. Deal one encounter card face down to each encounter tile, of the level the mini-boss's data card gives for that tile's position on the route.
new: 2. Deal one encounter card face down to each encounter tile, of the level the mini-boss's data card gives for that tile's position on the route. Keep the rest of each encounter deck face down beside the bonfire tile.
rationale: The encounter scry of §7.5 draws a replacement from the encounter deck, so the decks stay on the table.
evidence: §7.5, Encounter Resolution (scry); chapter 07 issues list, item 1.

old: 6. Place the mega-boss's model, *data card*, *health dial*, *behaviour cards*, and remaining boss treasure cards beside the game board.
new: 6. Place the mega-boss's model, *data card*, *health dial*, and remaining boss treasure cards beside the game board, build its *behaviour deck* as its rules direct (see §15.5; §17), and place the deck face down beside them.
rationale: A gravestone in the Level 4 encounter allows a scry of the next boss's behaviour deck, so the mega-boss's deck is built at setup as the other bosses' decks are (§6.5 step 7, §6.6 step 10).
evidence: §7.5, Encounter Resolution (scry); chapter 07 issues list, item 2.

old: When a weapon with Titanite attached is sold, the Titanite is returned with the weapon to the bottom of the treasure deck of the weapon's tier (see §11.4).
new: When a weapon with Titanite attached is sold, the Titanite is sold with it and adds nothing to the sell value. The weapon and the Titanite are separated, and each goes where a sold card of its kind goes (see §11.4, Sales).
rationale: One destination rule for every sold card: each card returns to the place of its own kind, as a replaced Titanite card already does (Appendix B).
evidence: Author's source 11_returning_to_the_bonfire.md (sold Titanite goes to the tier one deck); Appendix B, Titanite Replacement.

old: When a *weapon* with *Titanite* attached is sold, the Titanite goes with the weapon to the bottom of the treasure deck of the weapon's tier, and every other *upgrade card* attached to a sold card returns to the character's inventory (see §4.2, Titanite). The sell value of the weapon is paid once; attached Titanite adds nothing to it.
new: When a *weapon* with *Titanite* attached is sold, the Titanite is sold with it, and every other *upgrade card* attached to a sold card returns to the character's inventory (see §4.2, Titanite). The sell value of the weapon is paid once; attached Titanite adds nothing to it. The weapon and the Titanite are separated, and each goes to the place stated for a sold card of its kind.
rationale: As core-E31.

old: **Titanite.** A weapon upgrade (Titanite Shard, Titanite Chunk, Titanite Slab, or Titanite Scale) that is fused permanently to the weapon it is attached to. A Titanite Chunk is attached only in place of an attached Titanite Shard, and a Titanite Slab only in place of an attached Titanite Chunk; the replaced card returns to the bottom of the treasure deck of its tier (see Appendix B). When that weapon is sold, the Titanite is returned with it to the bottom of the treasure deck of the weapon's tier (see §4.2).
new: **Titanite.** A weapon upgrade card whose name includes the word Titanite (Titanite Shard, Titanite Chunk, Titanite Slab, Titanite Scale, Demon Titanite, and Blue Titanite), fused permanently to the weapon it is attached to. A Titanite Chunk is attached only in place of an attached Titanite Shard, and a Titanite Slab only in place of an attached Titanite Chunk; the replaced card returns to the bottom of the treasure deck of its tier (see Appendix B). When that weapon is sold, the Titanite is sold with it for no additional *souls*, and each card goes where a sold card of its kind goes (see §4.2; §11.4).
rationale: Carries both Titanite rulings: Titanite is recognised by name (core-063) and a sold Titanite card goes to the place of its own kind (core-048).

old: *Titanite* upgrade cards (Titanite Shard, Titanite Chunk, Titanite Slab, and Titanite Scale) are weapon upgrades that fuse permanently to the weapon they are attached to.
new: A *Titanite* card is a weapon upgrade card whose name includes the word Titanite: Titanite Shard, Titanite Chunk, Titanite Slab, Titanite Scale, Demon Titanite, and Blue Titanite. A Titanite card fuses permanently to the weapon it is attached to.
rationale: A test by name settles Demon Titanite and Blue Titanite without a second list: every card called Titanite behaves as Titanite.
evidence: Official 2017: no weapon upgrade is ever removed (DS-Core-Rules-lores.txt l.672-679); CMP-0004 labels both cards 'Weapon upgrade (Titanite)'.

old: - After an encounter is *cleared*, the party may return to the bonfire tile instead of advancing to the next tile (see §7.5, Encounter Recovery).
new: - After an encounter is *cleared*, the party may return to the bonfire tile and rest instead of advancing to the next tile (see §7.5, Encounter Recovery).
rationale: Returning and resting are one act, as §7.5 already states.
evidence: §7.5, Encounter Recovery; author's source 11_returning_to_the_bonfire.md l.8; official 2022 'Resting at the Bonfire' (DS-TG-Rulebook l.1927-1930, l.2075-2079).

old: Returning to the bonfire tile costs nothing. The party spends a *spark* only when it rests (see §11.2). Until the party rests, no character is restored, the Firekeeper and Andre cannot be visited, and no encounter is *reset*.
new: Returning to the bonfire tile and resting there are one act. The party returns only to rest, and the rest begins when the models are placed on the tile (see §11.2). The party cannot choose to return while the *spark* dial shows zero (see §7.4).
rationale: Removes the state of standing at the bonfire without resting, which had no use except to fight cleared encounters again without spending a spark.

old: **Bonfire.** The characters' safe haven, represented by the *bonfire* tile, which has no nodes. The Firekeeper and Blacksmith Andre wait there and are visited only while the party rests. Returning to the bonfire tile costs nothing; resting there costs one *spark* (see §11.1, §11.2).
new: **Bonfire.** The characters' safe haven, represented by the *bonfire* tile, which has no nodes. The Firekeeper and Blacksmith Andre wait there and are visited only while the party rests. The party returns to the bonfire tile only to rest, and a rest costs one *spark* unless it follows the defeat of a boss (see §11.1, §11.2).
rationale: Glossary follows §11.1.
